title: Ability and permission: 会, 能, 可以
summary: All three can translate as 'can'. 会 is a learned skill or a probability, 能 is physical or situational capacity, and 可以 is permission or possibility.
pattern: Subject + 会 / 能 / 可以 + Verb

rules.rule: **会 = know how to.** It describes a skill that was learned, such as languages, swimming or cooking. It also predicts what will probably happen: 会下雨.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ huì shuō yìdiǎnr Hànyǔ.
examples.english: I can speak a little Chinese.

examples.hanzi: 他会游泳，但是游得不快。
examples.pinyin: Tā huì yóuyǒng, dànshì yóu de bú kuài.
examples.english: He can swim, but not fast.

examples.pinyin: Míngtiān kěnéng huì xià yǔ.
examples.english: It may rain tomorrow.

rules.rule: **能 = be able to (in the circumstances).** The ability depends on health, time, rules or conditions at the moment. It is the normal word for quantities and limits.

examples.hanzi: 我感冒了，今天不能去上班。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ gǎnmào le, jīntiān bù néng qù shàngbān.
examples.english: I have a cold and cannot go to work today.

examples.hanzi: 他一分钟能打两百个字。
examples.pinyin: Tā yì fēnzhōng néng dǎ liǎng bǎi gè zì.
examples.english: He can type two hundred characters in a minute.

rules.rule: **可以 = be allowed / it is possible.** It asks and gives permission. The question is 可以…吗 or 可不可以; the refusal is 不可以 or the softer 不能.

examples.pinyin: Zhèlǐ kěyǐ tíngchē ma?
examples.english: May I park here?

examples.pinyin: Nǐ kěyǐ yòng wǒ de shǒujī.
examples.english: You may use my phone.

rules.rule: **Overlap:** 能 and 可以 are interchangeable for permission and for general possibility. Use **会** when you are talking about a skill and **能** when an outside condition decides. In a recovered ability, use 能: 病好了，我又能跑步了.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ néng bu néng xiǎoshēng yìdiǎnr?
examples.english: Could you keep your voice down a bit?

examples.hanzi: 他的腿好了，又能跑步了。
examples.pinyin: Tā de tuǐ hǎo le, yòu néng pǎobù le.
examples.english: His leg has healed and he can run again.

contrasts.text: English 'I can swim' is 我会游泳 (skill), 'I can swim today' (healthy enough) is 我今天能游泳. English has one word where Chinese distinguishes three sources of ability.
看得懂 / 听不见 express result-based ability. Use them instead of 能 + 懂 when the question is whether the result is reachable.

pitfalls: ✗ 我能说汉语。 (meant: I know Chinese) → ✓ 我会说汉语。 Learned skills use 会.
✗ 这里不会抽烟。 (meant: smoking is not allowed here) → ✓ 这里不能抽烟。 Prohibitions use 不能 / 不可以.
✗ 我会不会去。 (meant: can I come?) → ✓ 我可以去吗？ Asking permission calls for 可以.
✗ 我可以不会游泳。 → ✓ 我不会游泳。 Negate the modal itself, not the main verb.

title: Wanting and having to: 要, 想, 得, 需要
titleHanzi: 要 / 想 / 得 / 需要
summary: 想 is a wish, 要 is a firm plan or demand, and 得 (děi) or 需要 is an obligation. The negatives differ: 不想 'don't want', 不用 'needn't', 不要 'don't (or don't want)'.
pattern: Subject + 想 / 要 / 得 / 需要 + Verb

rules.rule: **想 + Verb** means 'would like to / feel like'. It is gentle and does not commit the speaker. With a noun object it means 'to miss' (想家).

examples.pinyin: Wǒ xiǎng hē yì bēi rè chá.
examples.english: I'd like a cup of hot tea.

examples.pinyin: Tā xiǎng xué kāichē.
examples.english: He wants to learn to drive.

rules.rule: **要 + Verb** means 'want to / will / have decided to'. It sounds more determined than 想 and is also the future marker. The negative is 不想 (not 不要, which means 'don't').

examples.pinyin: Wǒ yào qù Běijīng gōngzuò.
examples.english: I am going to work in Beijing.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ bù xiǎng qù, nǐ qù ba.
examples.english: I don't want to go; you go.

rules.rule: **得 (děi) + Verb** is the everyday 'have to'. It is spoken and strong; the negative is 不用 or 不必, never 不得 (which is formal for 'must not').

examples.pinyin: Shíjiān bù zǎo le, wǒ děi zǒu le.
examples.english: It's late, I have to go.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ míngtiān búyòng lái.
examples.english: You don't need to come tomorrow.

rules.rule: **需要 + Verb / Noun** says that something is needed: more formal and objective than 得, and also possible with nouns. 必须 is the next stage (see the lesson on 应该 and 必须).

examples.pinyin: Nǐ xūyào duō xiūxi.
examples.english: You need to rest more.

examples.pinyin: Zhège gōngzuò xūyào jīngyàn.
examples.english: This job requires experience.

contrasts.text: 想吃 'I feel like eating'; 要吃 'I will eat, I want to eat'. In a restaurant 我要 is the normal way to order, 我想 sounds like a polite suggestion.
要 + time can predict: 明天要下雨 (it is going to rain). With 了, 要…了 means 'about to'.

pitfalls: ✗ 我不要去。 (meant: I don't want to go) → ✓ 我不想去。 不要 as a command means 'don't'; for a refusal use 不想.
✗ 我得不去。 → ✓ 我不用去。 or 我不得不去。 得 is not negated with 不 after it.
✗ 我想要去北京。 → ✓ 我想去北京。 想要 + Verb is common and emphatic, while 想 is the standard everyday auxiliary for 'want to'.
✗ 我需要去吃饭。 → ✓ 我得去吃饭。 In speech 需要 sounds too formal for ordinary chores.

title: Advice and obligation: 应该, 该, 必须, 一定要
titleHanzi: 应该 / 必须 / 一定要
summary: 应该 gives advice or a reasonable expectation. 必须 states a strong obligation. 一定要 insists; 别 and 不必 are the ways to say it is not required.
pattern: Subject + 应该 / 该 / 必须 / 一定要 / 务必 + Verb

rules.rule: **应该 / 该** = should, ought to. It gives advice or morally right behaviour. It can also express an expectation about what is probably true.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ yīnggāi duō yùndòng.
examples.english: You should exercise more.

examples.hanzi: 他八点出发，现在应该到了。
examples.pinyin: Tā bā diǎn chūfā, xiànzài yīnggāi dào le.
examples.english: He left at eight, he should have arrived by now.

examples.pinyin: Háizi gāi shuìjiào le.
examples.english: It's time for the child to go to bed.

rules.rule: **必须** = must. It states a requirement from rules, logic or the situation. The negative is **不必 / 不用** ('need not'), not 不必须; a prohibition is **不能 / 不许**.

examples.pinyin: Zuò fēijī bìxū dài hùzhào.
examples.english: You must bring your passport when flying.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ búbì xiànzài huídá wǒ.
examples.english: You don't have to answer me now.

rules.rule: **一定要 / 务必** adds insistence from the speaker: 'make sure to'. 一定 alone can be a prediction ('surely'), 一定要 an order or a determination.

examples.pinyin: Míngtiān nǐ yídìng yào zhǔnshí lái.
examples.english: Be sure to come on time tomorrow.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ yídìng yào xuéhǎo Hànyǔ.
examples.english: I am determined to learn Chinese well.

rules.rule: **Softeners:** 最好 'had better', 得 for everyday must, 不得 / 不得不 in formal rules. 应该 can be strengthened by 完全 or softened by 可能.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ zuìhǎo dài yì bǎ sǎn.
examples.english: You had better take an umbrella.

examples.pinyin: Wèi jīng yǔnxǔ, bùdé rùnèi.
examples.english: No entry without permission.

contrasts.text: 不应该 means you should not (it is wrong), 不必须 does not exist. 必须 has no direct negative: use 不用 for 'not necessary' and 不能 for 'forbidden'.
得 is conversational; 必须 appears in rules, instructions and formal speech.

pitfalls: ✗ 你不必须来。 → ✓ 你不必来。 or 你不用来。 必须 cannot be negated directly.
✗ 你应该去了。 (meant: you should go) → ✓ 你应该去。 Advice does not take 了; 你应该去了 would say that he should already have gone.
✗ 你必须应该来。 → ✓ 你必须来。 One modal is enough.
✗ 一定你来。 → ✓ 你一定要来。 一定 is placed before the verb or modal, after the subject.

title: Willingness and nerve: 敢, 肯, 愿意
summary: These verbs describe the speaker's attitude toward doing something: dare to (敢), be willing to (肯, 愿意) and be glad to (乐意). Their negatives are common in everyday complaints.
pattern: Subject + 敢 / 肯 / 愿意 / 乐意 / 舍得 + Verb

rules.rule: **敢 + Verb** = dare. It is about courage: 不敢 'don't dare' is far more frequent than the positive. 敢 can also mean 'be bold enough to', admiring someone.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ bù gǎn yí gè rén zǒu yèlù.
examples.english: I dare not walk alone at night.

examples.hanzi: 他敢说真话，大家都很佩服。
examples.pinyin: Tā gǎn shuō zhēnhuà, dàjiā dōu hěn pèifú.
examples.english: He dares to tell the truth, and everyone admires him.

rules.rule: **肯 + Verb** = be willing to, agree to. It shows whether someone is ready to comply, and the negative 不肯 means 'refuse (stubbornly)'.

examples.pinyin: Tā bù kěn gàosu wǒ zhēnxiàng.
examples.english: He refuses to tell me the truth.

examples.hanzi: 只要你肯努力，一定能成功。
examples.pinyin: Zhǐyào nǐ kěn nǔlì, yídìng néng chénggōng.
examples.english: As long as you are willing to work hard, you will certainly succeed.

rules.rule: **愿意 + Verb** = be willing to, would like to. It can be used with a person as object or with a clause. It is more neutral and more polite than 肯.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ yuànyì gēn wǒ yìqǐ qù ma?
examples.english: Would you be willing to go with me?

examples.pinyin: Wǒ yuànyì bāng nǐ de máng.
examples.english: I'm happy to help you.

rules.rule: **舍得 / 舍不得** and **乐意** colour the feeling: 舍得 'not mind spending / parting with', 舍不得 'hate to part with', 乐意 'gladly'.

examples.pinyin: Tā shěbude líkāi jiāxiāng.
examples.english: She cannot bear to leave her hometown.

examples.pinyin: Tā shěde huā qián mǎi hǎo shū.
examples.english: He doesn't mind spending money on good books.

contrasts.text: 想 is a personal wish, 愿意 is agreement to a proposal: 你愿意嫁给我吗？ (will you), not 你想嫁给我吗.
我不敢去 means I'm too afraid to go; 我不能去 means something prevents me from going.

pitfalls: ✗ 我不愿意去，因为我愿意不去。 → ✓ 我不愿意去。 Do not stack an attitude verb on top of a negated verb unless the double meaning is intended.
✗ 他敢不敢吗？ → ✓ 他敢不敢？ Same as other A-not-A questions: no 吗.
✗ 我肯去了。 → ✓ 我愿意去。 肯 usually appears in negative or conditional sentences, rarely as a plain positive.
✗ 我舍不得离开了。 → ✓ 我舍不得离开。 No 了 after an attitude verb in a general statement.

title: Negating modal verbs: 不能, 不可以, 不用, 别
titleHanzi: 不能 / 不可以 / 不用 / 不必
summary: Negating a modal does not always give its logical opposite. 不用 is not 'must not', and 必须 has no direct negative. This article maps each modal to the right negative.
pattern: Modal → negative: 会 → 不会 · 能 → 不能 · 可以 → 不可以 / 不能 · 要 (obligation) → 不用 · 必须 → 不必 / 不用 · 应该 → 不应该

rules.rule: **Ability:** 不会 (can't, never learned), 不能 (can't now). **Permission:** 不能 or 不可以 (not allowed); 不可以 is firmer and more formal.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ bú huì kāichē.
examples.english: I can't drive.

examples.hanzi: 在图书馆里不能大声说话。
examples.pinyin: Zài túshūguǎn lǐ bù néng dàshēng shuōhuà.
examples.english: You must not talk loudly in the library.

rules.rule: **Obligation:** The logical opposite of 'must' is 'need not', which is 不用 / 不必 / 用不着. To say 'must not' use 不能 / 不许 / 别 instead.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ búyòng zháojí, shíjiān hái zǎo.
examples.english: No need to hurry, it's still early.

examples.pinyin: Zhèlǐ bù xǔ pāizhào.
examples.english: Taking photos is not allowed here.

rules.rule: **Advice:** 不应该 / 不该 means 'should not', which is a moral judgement: 你不应该骗人. Note that 别 is the command form.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ bù yīnggāi zhèyàng duì péngyou.
examples.english: You shouldn't treat your friends like this.

examples.pinyin: Bié piàn rén!
examples.english: Don't lie!

rules.rule: **Wish and courage:** 不想 (don't feel like), 不要 (don't want or don't), 不敢 (dare not), 不肯 (refuse), 不愿意 (unwilling). The meaning of the negative shifts with the verb.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ bù xiǎng chī le, yǐjīng bǎo le.
examples.english: I don't want to eat any more, I'm already full.

examples.pinyin: Tā bù kěn dàoqiàn.
examples.english: He refuses to apologise.

contrasts.text: English 'You mustn't go' = 你不能去; English 'You don't have to go' = 你不用去. In Chinese the second one is not simply a shifted negation.
Modal verbs are negated with 不 only. For a past 'did not manage to', use 没能 or 没有 + complement: 我没能去。

pitfalls: ✗ 你不必须去。 → ✓ 你不用去。 必须 cannot be negated with 不.
✗ 昨天我不能去。 (meant: I wasn't able to) → ✓ 昨天我没能去。 or 昨天我没法去。 A past inability uses 没能.
✗ 我不会不去。 as a refusal → ✓ 我不去。 不会不 means 'I won't fail to', a double negation.
✗ 你不要去吗？ (meant: don't you want to go?) → ✓ 你不想去吗？ 不要 sounds like a command here.
